title: Starting a band by ear: simple blues, chords and parts
summary: DeVore explains how to get beginners playing: take melody and chords off records, start with a blues and simple parts for piano, trombone, clarinet and cornet, and learn chords as Johnny Wiggs showed him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, I don't know exactly what you want, but... Neither do we. If you're just interested in the band aspect as opposed against the individual aspect, there's a few simple little things that can be done to make it pretty fundamental. Now, I think, from my own experience anyway, you've got to have one or two guys with fairly sharp ears if you're going to learn the various tunes. And for musicians that aren't from New Orleans and haven't heard the tunes, the only way they can pick them up is from records, of course. And you have to take melody and the chords from the records. That's where you start. And you've got anybody that can't play. Explain that. I say you have to take the melodies of the tunes and the chords from the tunes probably off the records, even if a guy couldn't play anything. I mean, that's where you'd have to start. And then, once you got the chords... Well, take a simple tune, for instance. Just the blues. That's the way we did it. The fellas that I ran into in Minneapolis were reading these Dixonland arrangements from books, you know. The books that you can buy in New York. They're published in New York. All these fancy Dixonland arrangements. And most of them, they had some experience in reading, but they never tried to muck you around faking it or just ear music. So what I did was show the piano player the very basic blues chords, you know. Tonic and subdominant and dominant and tonic. And then we went from there. Told them just to whack it out four beats to the bar for 12 bars of blues. And I played a simple blues line, and I told the trombone player just to fill in basically what the piano player would be doing in his left hand. And then I told the clarinet player to start playing eighth notes. This is just a very basic beginning without any of the embellishments of jazz music in there. Just running eighth notes from the top of the scale down and back up again to get the driving feeling that the New Orleans clarinetists do. It's a lot more complex than that, but basically that's what they're doing. And we did that for a blues tune and then ran across another tune they might know and did basically the same thing, but over 16 bars or 32 bars on that order. But that was the basic thing for us. We'd get the piano player to sit down in front of the piano and just beat out four beats to the bar. Just bonk, bonk, bonk, bonk, bonk. And then work the trombone part and the clarinet part around that. Of course it goes without saying that the cornet man or the trumpet man would have to know the melody and play it just about as straight as possible. It would sound awfully square at first, and it's not until you get the basic ideas of what has to be done first before you can start putting in some of the other things.
